Steel prep: scale off, paint on

What gets cleaned, in what order, and what goes on it afterwards. No steel face is left bare — every steel part lands against 6061 and the aluminium is the anode, and the plate that faces out is the one the wet chips land on. The scheme is self-etch primer on the mating faces, 2K poly clear on the show faces, which keeps the raw steel look on everything that is visible.

The parts

Part Stock What is on it as it arrives
Two Y outboard plates 10 gauge cold-rolled steel sheet mill oil, and flash rust on the waterjet edges and hole walls
Y rear plate, one for both beams 1/4" hot-rolled A36 mill scale, unless it was bought P&O
Two Y nut sole brackets 1/4" A36, the same sheet as the rear plate mill scale

Every one of them is already cut — the steel went to the waterjet and none of it is on the mill trip — so prep and paint happen before any of it is bolted up.

SETTLED: It is done at home, in a can, not sent out for powder. Powder would come back finished and opaque, and the show faces are staying raw steel.

1 — Degrease before the first abrasive touches it

FLAG: Oil first, abrasive second, and not the other way round. Cold-rolled sheet ships with a rust-preventive oil on it. Sand it first and the oil is driven into the surface, nothing bonds to it afterwards, and there is nothing to see — the plate looks the same as one that was done properly.

Acetone or denatured alcohol on a rag, changing rags as they load up. Or hot water and dish soap with a scrub pad, then towel dry and a heat gun pass straight away — bare wet steel starts rusting in minutes.

2 — Take the surface down

Part Tool
1/4" hot-rolled — rear plate, sole brackets 60–80 grit flap disc on an angle grinder, or a wire cup brush. Scale is harder than the steel under it and kills sandpaper
10 gauge cold-rolled — outboard plates 120–180 grit, or a maroon abrasive pad. There is no scale here; you are only putting tooth on it for the primer
Every waterjet edge and hole wall abrasive pad or a nylon brush, and get inside the holes

The waterjet cuts wet, so the edges and hole walls carry light flash rust even when the faces look clean.

A phosphoric acid metal prep gel is the alternative to the grinder on the scale, and it leaves a phosphate layer the primer likes. Slower, and it has to be rinsed and dried.

The stains a maroon pad will not take out

A pad or a sander leaves the faces clean except for the odd mark that looks like a water stain and stays. Three different things look identical, so test before working on them:

Test What it means
Acetone on a white rag — if the rag colours, or the mark's edge moves It is oil residue, not oxide. Denatured alcohol is weak on rolling oil, and a maroon pad burnishes a ring rather than lifting it. This is the one that kills paint adhesion
150–180 grit on a hard block, a dozen strokes — if it clears It was only on the surface. A maroon pad is non-woven, so it conforms, polishes the high spots and rides over anything sitting below them. A rigid backing cuts flat and reaches it
It survives both It is in a shallow pit. Water sat there and the oxide went in below the surface

FLAG: Stop sanding a pitted stain. Reaching the bottom of the pit means taking all the metal around it down to that depth, which is real thickness off the panel for a mark that paint covers.

Those go to phosphoric acid instead — naval jelly for spot work because the gel stays where it is put, Ospho or a prep-and-etch for a wipe-on, or Evapo-Rust and citric acid, which chelate rather than etch and so leave the good metal alone. For a stain in the middle of a face that is already good, soak a paper towel, lay it on, and cover it with plastic so it cannot dry out.

The acid turns the oxide into iron phosphate — a grey-black inert layer, and a better primer substrate than the bright steel beside it. So treating a stain improves the panel rather than repairing it, and the patch staying darker than its surround does not matter under primer.

FLAG: Rinsed with water, it flash rusts in minutes. Either use a product meant to be left to dry, or rinse, heat gun it dry straight away, and prime the same day.

3 — Deburr while it is still bare

The waterjet leaves a lip on the exit side of a hole. Hand countersink or a deburring tool, both faces of every hole, and file the sheared edges.

FLAG: Do it now. A hole opened out or an edge filed after the paint is on is bare steel in the one place that is hardest to reach again.

4 — Solvent wipe, then gloves

Acetone or lacquer thinner on a lint-free rag, immediately before the primer goes on. Nitrile gloves from that wipe onwards. A fingerprint is salt and oil, and it is reliably where the first bloom comes through the film.

5 — Prime inside the hour

Freshly abraded steel flash rusts in hours. The window is short enough that the can wants to be shaken and ready before step 4, not after.

Rust-Oleum Automotive Self Etching Primer, dark grey. A rust converting primer goes on first anywhere pitting is left after step 2.
Coats 2 or 3 thin, 2 minutes apart
Dry to touch 10 min
Dry to handle 15–30 min
Before the topcoat 30 min minimum
Before dry sanding 3–4 hours
Conditions 50–90 °F, humidity under 85 %
Coverage 10–12 sq ft a can — the mating faces and edges alone are about a canful, so have three

FLAG: It is a tie coat, not a finish. Self-etch is thin and porous by design — it bites bare metal and gives the next layer something to hold. Dark grey looks finished enough to stop at, and on its own it is not the moisture barrier that is the whole job at these joints. Something goes over it, even cheap enamel on a face nobody sees.

FLAG: Nothing gets sprayed in a room with the mining rigs running. They move enough air to lay dust into wet primer through the ten minutes it takes to flash, and an aerosol puts a solvent vapour cloud around energised electronics with fans in it. Spray elsewhere, or shut them down and ventilate first.

FLAG: A sacrificial zinc-rich primer is the wrong choice at these joints. What is wanted between steel and aluminium is an insulating film, not a more active metal put deliberately into the circuit.

6 — Two finishes, and no bare metal left anywhere

The show faces stay raw steel under 2K poly clear. The mating faces get the primer. Nothing is left bare: the outboard plate is the chip barrier, so it is the part that actually gets wet.

Face What goes on it
Mating face — against the beam Self-etch primer, then anything over it. Nobody sees it, so cheap enamel does
Show face 2K poly clear, straight onto the bare steel
Edges and hole walls Clear, not primer. They take the thinnest film and are where failure starts

The edges go to the clear and the primer stops at the mating face. Wrapping grey primer round onto a show face leaves a band you can see through the clear, and the clear seals the edge just as well. Two thin coats beat one heavy one either way — a heavy coat pulls away from an edge as it flows.

FLAG: Nothing goes under the clear that you are not keeping. Every stain, fingerprint and bit of flash rust left on a show face is sealed in and permanent, and there is no second attempt. Settle step 2 on those faces before the can is opened. This is the one place the stains stop being cosmetic.

FLAG: There is no primer under the clear, so the clear is the only thing holding. Bare steel is the weakest substrate a 2K urethane gets asked to grip — the sanding key is all it has, and a breach lets rust creep under the film where it cannot be reached. Which is the price of the raw look, and it is paid in keeping the surface clean before spraying rather than in anything added afterwards.

Order it so the clear is one session. Prime every mating face first and leave them to cure. A 2K can is activated once, has a pot life measured in a day or two, and cannot be saved — so every show face gets done in one go, after the primer is hard.

FLAG: 2K hardener is isocyanate. It is a respiratory sensitiser, the kind of exposure that makes the next one worse rather than the kind you get used to. Cartridge respirator at the absolute minimum, strong ventilation, and nowhere near the mining rigs.

Bare-metal protectants are not primer

A graphene or wax film — Carbon Coat, Boeshield T-9, paste wax — protects a surface that has to stay bare: a cast iron table, a bed, a tool. It is a thin film, it is meant to be renewed, and standing water still gets through it. None of that is what a steel plate bolted flat to aluminium for a metre needs, and the film has to come off again before primer would stick to it.

Use one only on steel that is waiting, and plan on removing it:
Carbon Coat the best of the three against ambient humidity on bare metal, and it is a friction reducer, so nothing primes over it
Boeshield T-9 or LPS-3 thin waxy film, months indoors
Paste wax dry to the touch and the easiest to take off again, with mineral spirits
Lanolin longest hold, messiest

While they wait

Store the plates on edge, off the concrete. A slab wicks moisture into anything laid flat on it, and the down face goes first.

One that belongs at assembly

FLAG: Paint creeps under sustained bolt load, so a painted joint loses bolt tension. Re-check the torque on the outboard plates and the rear plate a few weeks after they go on.
